variants.title: Pick the scaling axis
variants.context: Replication stores copies of the same keys on several nodes. Sharding gives each node a different ownership range. Adding replicas does not divide one shard’s writes; losing a shard is not covered by the other shards.
variants.prompt: One tenant’s writes are overloading its shard. Which change actually divides that tenant’s write load?
options: Route the tenant’s reads to the nearest replica.
Add two more replicas to the busy shard.
Split the tenant’s key range across more shards.
optionFeedback: Read routing changes where reads go; it leaves the write stream on the same primary.
Replicas copy the same keys, so every replica still receives every one of the tenant’s writes.
Only a new ownership range divides writes. Splitting the tenant’s keys gives the load a second owner.
variants.hint: Ask whether the problem is too many copies of the same keys or too few owners of different keys.
variants.explanation: Writes divide only across ownership ranges. Splitting the tenant’s keys across shards gives its write load more than one owner; replicas would copy the same load.

variants.title: Pick the scaling axis
variants.context: Replication stores copies of the same keys on several nodes. Sharding gives each node a different ownership range. Adding replicas does not divide one shard’s writes; losing a shard is not covered by the other shards.
variants.prompt: A zone outage takes a shard’s only copy offline, and its records disappear from the application. Which plan prevents that next time?
options: Increase the number of shards in the cluster.
Keep replicas of each shard in separate failure domains.
Rehash all keys with a different hash function.
optionFeedback: More shards spread different keys; none of them holds the lost shard’s records.
Replicas in separate failure domains keep a copy readable when one zone is lost.
A new hash moves keys between owners; it creates no extra copy of any key.
variants.hint: Losing data means there was no second copy. Which axis adds copies?
variants.explanation: Availability of a shard comes from copies in independent failure domains, not from more shards. Every shard needs a copy plan as well as an ownership plan.

variants.title: Pick the scaling axis
variants.context: Replication stores copies of the same keys on several nodes. Sharding gives each node a different ownership range. Adding replicas does not divide one shard’s writes; losing a shard is not covered by the other shards.
variants.prompt: Catalog reads are twenty times the writes and may be a few seconds stale. Which change adds read capacity with the least data movement?
options: Send every catalog read to the shard primary.
Add read replicas and route catalog reads to them.
Re-shard the catalog by a new key.
optionFeedback: The primary already serves the writes; adding all reads concentrates load on it.
Replicas serve permitted reads without moving ownership; bounded staleness is acceptable here.
Re-sharding moves data and changes ownership; it adds write capacity you do not need.
variants.hint: The workload is read-heavy and staleness-tolerant. Which axis copies keys instead of moving them?
variants.explanation: Read replicas add read capacity for the same keys without moving ownership. Re-sharding is for write or storage limits.

variants.title: Diagnose the shard key
variants.context: A shard key chooses the owner of each record. A strong key has high cardinality, even activity, query locality, stable ownership, and can be split later.
variants.prompt: Orders are range-sharded by created_at. Every new order lands on the same shard while older shards sit idle. Which shard-key property is missing?
options: High cardinality of key values.
Stable ownership of each record.
Even activity across key values.
optionFeedback: There are plenty of distinct timestamps; the problem is that the newest ones are all hot at once.
Timestamps never change after creation, so ownership is stable. The imbalance is about activity.
A monotonically increasing key sends all new writes to the active end of the range layout.
variants.hint: There are millions of distinct timestamps. What do the busiest ones have in common?
variants.explanation: A monotonic timestamp has high cardinality but uneven activity: the newest values are hot together, so one range owner takes almost every write.

variants.title: Diagnose the shard key
variants.context: A shard key chooses the owner of each record. A strong key has high cardinality, even activity, query locality, stable ownership, and can be split later.
variants.prompt: A table is sharded by country code. There are forty countries, and three of them carry most of the traffic. What is the main problem?
options: Range scans scatter across shards.
The key changes whenever a profile is edited.
Low cardinality leaves only a few busy owners.
optionFeedback: Country codes group records; scans by country stay local. The problem is how few owners there are.
Country rarely changes; stability is not the issue here.
Forty values cannot spread load across many owners, and three hot values dominate the few that exist.
variants.hint: Count the distinct values the router has to work with.
variants.explanation: A low-cardinality field gives the router only a handful of owners, and skewed traffic makes a few of them hot.

variants.title: Diagnose the shard key
variants.context: A shard key chooses the owner of each record. A strong key has high cardinality, even activity, query locality, stable ownership, and can be split later.
variants.prompt: Sharding by tenant_id keeps each tenant’s reads local, but one enterprise tenant is 60% of all traffic. Which fix divides that tenant while keeping locality for the rest?
options: Add a bucket suffix for the large tenant.
Switch every tenant to random hashing.
Add replicas to the large tenant’s shard.
optionFeedback: Bucketing spreads one logical key across owners; reads over that tenant must fan out and merge.
Random hashing destroys locality for every small tenant to fix one large one.
Replicas copy the tenant’s writes; they do not divide them.
variants.hint: Which change splits one logical key without changing the contract for everyone else?
variants.explanation: A bucket suffix splits the dominant tenant across owners. The cost is fan-out on that tenant’s reads, which is a fair trade for keeping the others local.

variants.title: Size the shard count
variants.context: Each shard can sustain a known peak write rate. Plan so the hottest expected owner stays below its limit with headroom for failure and rebalancing.
variants.prompt: Peak load is 18,000 writes/second. One shard sustains 4,000 writes/second, and you must keep 30% headroom. Assuming even spread, how many shards do you need?
variants.hint: Multiply peak by 1.3 for headroom, divide by per-shard capacity, then round up.
variants.explanation: 18,000 × 1.3 = 23,400 writes/second. 23,400 ÷ 4,000 = 5.85, so six shards. Uneven activity would raise this number.

mistakes.feedback: Five shards cover the raw peak but leave no headroom for a lost node or a rebalance.
Round up: you cannot run half a shard.
That divides 18,000 by 4,000 without the 30% headroom and forgets to round up.

variants.title: Size the shard count
variants.context: Each shard can sustain a known peak write rate. Plan so the hottest expected owner stays below its limit with headroom for failure and rebalancing.
variants.prompt: Peak load is 25,000 writes/second. One shard sustains 6,000 writes/second, and you must keep 20% headroom. Assuming even spread, how many shards do you need?
variants.hint: Multiply peak by 1.2 for headroom, divide by per-shard capacity, then round up.

mistakes.feedback: Round up to whole shards, and include the headroom first.
That divides 25,000 by 6,000 with no headroom and rounds down.
Six is safe but more than the plan requires: 30,000 ÷ 6,000 is exactly five.

variants.title: Size the shard count
variants.context: Each shard can sustain a known peak write rate. Plan so the hottest expected owner stays below its limit with headroom for failure and rebalancing.
variants.prompt: Peak load is 9,000 writes/second. One shard sustains 2,500 writes/second, and you must keep 50% headroom. Assuming even spread, how many shards do you need?
variants.hint: Multiply peak by 1.5 for headroom, divide by per-shard capacity, then round up.

mistakes.feedback: That covers 9,000 writes/second with no headroom at all.
5.4 rounds up, not down; five shards would exceed capacity during a rebalance.

variants.title: Route the read
variants.context: Routing picks an eligible replica per operation. Nearest-replica reads favor latency but can be stale; session-aware reads wait for a replica to reach the write’s position; primary-only or quorum reads favor current data at a latency cost.
variants.prompt: A user saves a profile change and immediately reloads. Reads normally go to the nearest replica. Which policy keeps the reload correct without moving all reads to the primary?
options: Nearest-replica reads with a longer cache TTL.
Primary-only reads for every request.
Session-aware reads that wait for the write position.
optionFeedback: A longer TTL makes the stale profile last longer, not shorter.
Primary-only reads would be correct, but they move every read to the primary and pay its latency; the question asked to avoid that.
Carrying the write position lets the router use a replica only once it has applied that write.
variants.hint: The reader knows exactly which write it needs to see.
variants.explanation: Session-aware reads carry the write’s position. The router serves from a replica that has reached it, otherwise waits briefly or falls back to the primary.

variants.title: Route the read
variants.context: Routing picks an eligible replica per operation. Nearest-replica reads favor latency but can be stale; session-aware reads wait for a replica to reach the write’s position; primary-only or quorum reads favor current data at a latency cost.
variants.prompt: A payment authorization runs right after an account lock and must not observe the pre-lock state. Which read policy fits?
options: Primary-only reads, or a quorum read.
Nearest-replica reads for low latency.
Any replica, retried until the answer changes.
optionFeedback: The authorization needs current data; a primary or a protocol-defined quorum provides it.
A nearby replica can lag behind the lock and approve a payment it should refuse.
Retrying a stale replica adds latency and still cannot prove it has caught up.
variants.hint: Which operation here cannot tolerate bounded staleness?
variants.explanation: The read policy belongs to the operation. A payment check after a lock needs the authority’s current state, so it reads from the primary or through the protocol’s quorum rule.

variants.title: Route the read
variants.context: Routing picks an eligible replica per operation. Nearest-replica reads favor latency but can be stale; session-aware reads wait for a replica to reach the write’s position; primary-only or quorum reads favor current data at a latency cost.
variants.prompt: A product catalog page is latency-sensitive and can show data that is a few seconds old. Which read policy fits?
options: Nearest-replica reads.
Primary-only reads.
Quorum reads on every request.
optionFeedback: Nearest replicas give the lowest latency, and bounded staleness is acceptable for browsing.
The primary is correct but slower and pauses during promotion; browsing does not need it.
Quorum reads spend several round trips for a freshness guarantee the page does not need.
variants.hint: Match the policy to what this operation can tolerate.
variants.explanation: Catalog browsing tolerates bounded staleness, so nearest-replica reads win on latency and read scale.
